1


REPLY BRIEF
The Kentucky Supreme Court held that prohibiting a group of Catholics from erecting a shrine to the
Virgin Mary on their own land does not impose a substantial burden because they could build a smaller
shrine elsewhere and because they were aware of the
prohibitory ordinance before applying to the zoning
board.  It also held that an ordinance that facially favors country clubs and rec centers over houses of worship does not violate the Equal Terms Provision.  Both
holdings lie on the extreme end of longstanding fractures among lower courts over RLUIPA’s land -use
provisions.
Although respondents claim that petitioner would
not prevail under  any standard adopted by lower
courts, they  acknowledge that the Third Circuit recently issued an on -point decision adopting  petitioner’s arguments  on the first question presented.
Anash v. Borough of Kingston , 184 F.4th 214, 236-37
(2026).  And respondents are forced to rewrite the decision below to justify it under existing standards—
claiming, for example,  that the Kentucky Supreme
Court discerned a “traffic -based line” in the challenged ordinance when it said no such thing.
Finally, respondents’ vehicle concerns are baseless.  Their “adequate and independent state ground”
is really an alternative federal ground for affirmance.
And their  invited-error objection confuses an argument made in the alternative with affirmative endorsement.

2


I. THE COURT SHOULD GRANT REVIEW ON
THE SUBSTANTIAL-BURDEN QUESTION
A. Respondents offer no persuasive defense of the
Kentucky Supreme Court’s  substantial-burden holding, which relied on the “alternative” of constructing a
smaller grotto elsewhere and on petitioner’s awareness of the prohibitory ordinance when it applied for
a permit.  Pet. App. 25a-27a.
With respect  to the  purported alternative, respondents say ( BIO 25) that “ whether the claimant
could engage in the same exercise ” without “running
afoul of the regulation” is relevant to whether the regulation is a substantial burden  (quotation omitted).
But as petitioner explained, RLUIPA is property-specific:  It defines the use of real property for religious
purposes as itself a “religious exercise of the person or
entity that uses or intends to use the property for that
purpose.”  42 U.S.C. § 2000cc -5(7)(B) (emphasis
added).  Completely prohibiting the use of property for
a specific religious activity is a substantial burden on
that statutorily defined religious exercise, even if the
owner could acquire other land for that activity.
As the Third Circuit has explained, “through
RLUIPA’s land -use substantial  burden provision,
Congress codified a basic principle: except  when the
implementation of a land use regulation satisfies
strict scrutiny, the choice of where the exercise of religion can take place should be left to persons with
rights of access to and use of real property—not to zoning codes and landmarking laws promulgated by governments.”  Anash, 184 F.4th at 244 .  Respondents
offer no answer to that point, which accords with the
settled principle that “the exercise of [one’s] liberty of
expression” may not be “abridged on the plea that it

3


may be exercised in some other place ,” Schneider v.
State, 308 U.S. 147, 163 (1939).
Even if alternative locations could sometimes dispel a substantial burden, that is clearly not true here.
Petitioner believes, based on the circumstances of the
Virgin’s apparition at Lourdes, that “it is God’s will to
build this shrine * * * on its property next to Our Lady
of Lourdes Church” and that it has “no feasible alternative location from which it can carry on this particular mission.”  Supp. App. 10a-11a.  The Kentucky
Supreme Court did not dispute those statements of religious faith, observing only that petitioner “has not
asserted that it could not construct a smaller grotto or
shrine on the property it already owned .”  Pet. App.
25a.  But when it comes to religious structures, building a smaller version is simply not the same exercise
of religion.  A chapel is not the same thing as a cathedral.  And this Court has long cautioned against permitting the government, or a reviewing court, to
second-guess how a religious adherent defines his own
religious exercise.  See Thomas v. Review Bd. of Ind.
Emp’t Sec. Div., 450 U.S. 707, 714-16 (1981).
Further, petitioner submitted unrebutted evidence
that expanding within the existing plot would have required excavating the parking lot, and the ordinance’s
own setback requirements would confine any structure to the middle of that lot.  Supp. App. 15a.  Tearing
up the church parking lot would obviously be a substantial burden under any standard.
As for the Kentucky Supreme Court’s other rationale, respondents argue  (BIO 23-24) that a restriction is not “impose [d]” by the “government”
within the meaning of RLUIPA, 42 U.S.C.
§ 2000cc(a)(1), if the government enacted the

4


restriction before the RLUIPA claimant acquired the
property.  In no other legal context would that reasoning be accepted.  A legal  prohibition enacted by the
government is “imposed” by the government even if a
citizen is aware of it before acting.
At any rate, respondents agree (BIO 24) that it is
irrelevant “ whether the organization knew about a
given regulation when it asked for a variance .”  Yet
that is exactly what the Kentucky Supreme Court
held.  Pet. App. 27a.  Respondents’ claim (BIO 12) that
the court relied on what petitioner knew when it
“leased” the property is found nowhere in the opinion.
2.  It is widely acknowledged that appellate courts
have adopted inconsistent standards for a substantial
burden.  Pet. 18-27; see also, e.g., Anash, 184 F.4th at
236 n.17.  Respondents do not deny the longstanding
conflict.  Instead, they argue (BIO 11 -23) that all
courts give weight to the same two considerations as
the decision below.
That is incorrect.  Most clearly, the Third Circuit’s
recent precedential decision in Anash, supra, rejected
both considerations.  In an opinion written by Judge
Phipps and joined by Judge Mascott, the court reversed the denial of a preliminary injunction against
enforcement of a commercial -zoning ordinance to
block the use of buildings for religious purposes.   184
F.4th at 224 .  The court held  that RLUIPA “has no
provisions for scrutinizing the actions or expectations
of persons seeking to exercise religion,” id. at 239 n.21,
and that a plaintiff does “not need to disprove the feasibility of alternative locations” to show a substantial
burden, id. at 245.  In a holding directly on point, the
Third Circuit concluded that “in all but the most dire
circumstances, a land use  regulation that prevents

5


access to or use of real property for  religious exercise
will contravene RLUIPA —regardless of the presence
of feasible alternative locations for the religious exercise.”  Id. at 244.  The court acknowledged the circuit
conflict, id. at 244 n.31, and Judge Restrepo dissented
on that basis, id. at 251-52.
Respondents claim (BIO 22-23) that the Third Circuit’s statutory interpretation would not bind future
panels given the preliminary -injunction posture, but
their own authority indicates the opposite: “If the first
panel does not stop at the question of likelihood of success and instead addresses the merits, the later
panel . . .  should regard itself as bound by the prior
panel opinion.”  Pitt News v. Pappert, 379 F.3d 96, 105
(3d Cir. 2004) (Alito, J.); cf. Nat’l Insts. of Health v.
Am. Pub. Health Assn., 145 S. Ct. 2658, 2663 (2025)
(Gorsuch, J., concurring in part and dissenting in
part) (“[R]egardless of a decision’s procedural posture,
its reasoning—its ratio decidendi—carries precedential weight in future cases.” ) (quotation omitted).
Anash’s statutory interpretation (as opposed to its application of that interpretation to the facts) was not
limited to a “likelihood” standard .  See 184 F.4th at
235-45.
Anash aside, both the Second and Ninth Circuit s
have rejected the proposition that the “alternative” of
constructing a structure in a different area forecloses
a substantial burden  where size and practical constraints render the location material to the exercise of
religion.  See Pet. 26-27.  Respondents cite (BIO 13-
15) decisions from those circuits consider ing alternative locations.  But in the one cited decision finding no
substantial burden, the change in location w as not
material to the religious practice .  See New Harvest

6


Christian Fellowship v. City of Salinas, 29 F.4th 596,
605 (9th Cir. 2022), cert. denied, 143 S. Ct. 567 (2023).
Respondents have identified no case involving a burden remotely similar to the burden here—forcing a religious community to build a smaller shrine in a
different location.  Moreover, the Second Circuit has
explained a RLUIPA claimant need not negate every
conceivable alternative, but only those “ quick, reliable, and financially feasible alternatives ” that “ meet
its religious needs.”  Westchester Day Sch. v. Village of
Mamaroneck, 504 F.3d 338, 352 (2d Cir. 2007).   A
smaller shrine in the church parking lot does not satisfy that standard.
With respect to the Kentucky Supreme Court’s
other justification, respondents cite no case endorsing
the view that merely submitting a  land-use application with foreknowledge of a prohibition makes the injury “self-imposed.”  And respondents do not contend
that the Second and Ninth Circuits  hold that  foreknowledge of the ban before acquiring property would
alone foreclose a substantial burden.
C.   Respondents raise two purported vehicle problems on the first question presented, but they are both
illusory.
1. Respondents claim (BIO 27) that petitioner invited the error by arguing in favor of the Sixth Circuit’s Livingston standard below.  That is mistaken.
In its Kentucky Supreme Court merits brief, petitioner argued in the alternative  that it could satisfy
the tests adopted by every circuit, including the Sixth
Circuit.  Supp. App. 1a-4a.  But its primary argument
was the same argument it raises here: “Denial of [Petitioner’s] permit would have acted as a complete

7


prohibition of its religious exercise .”  Supp. App.  4a
(capitalization altered) .  And  after a comprehensive
textual analysis, Supp. App.  4a-5a, petitioner  cited
the same Second Circuit decision that it cites here as
supplying a favorable standard, Supp. App. 5a-6a (citing Westchester Day Sch., 504 F.3d  at 349), as well as
a Third Circuit decision explaining that “[t]here can
hardly be a more substantial burden on a religious
practice or exercise than its outright prohibition,” Davis v. Wigen , 82 F. 4th 204, 212 (3d Cir. 2023) (cited
Supp. App. 5a); see also Supp. App. 6a-9a (citing Sixth
and Ninth Circuit decisions in the RLUIPA prisoner
context).
Only in its tertiary argument did petitioner state
that it could also prevail under the Livingston factors,
without claiming  that Livingston articulates the
proper standard.  Supp. App. 9a-10a.  While respondents quote (BIO 8) the word “agree[d]” in the opinion
below in a manner that suggests that the Kentucky
Supreme Court was agreeing with petitioner about
the Livingston standard, the court actually stated
that it “agreed with the Frederics’ assertion that
the * * * Livingston [standard] * * * should be our
polestar,” Pet. App. 22a (emphasis added).
Respondents also point (BIO 27)  to a  statement
from petitioner’s motion for discretionary review below (equivalent to a certiorari petition)  that Livingston was a “more appropriate” standard than the
standard applied by the court of appeals .  B ut the
Kentucky Supreme Court did not deem that statement to have forfeited petitioner’s merits arguments—and respondents did not so argue below.  That
forfeited state-law procedural objection has no bearing on this Court’s review.

8


2.  Respondents claim (BIO 27 -28) that the decision below is supported by an  “adequate and independent state ground.”  That is not correct.
  An adequate and independent state ground must
“independently and adequately support [] the judgment.”  Michigan v. Long, 463 U.S. 1032, 1038 (1983)
(quotation omitted) .  Respondents point (BIO 27) to
the court of appeals’ holding  that the Board lacked
statutory authority to grant the conditional -use permit.  The Kentucky Supreme Court declined to uphold
the lower court’s decision on that basis, and with good
reason:  If RLUIPA prohibits denial of the permit, that
overrides state law and entitle s petitioner to judgment.
Respondents, however, claim that the state -law
holding necessarily means that the Substantial Burden Provision does not apply here.  Section
2000cc(a)(2) limits that provision to burdens that affect interstate commerce, relate to a federally funded
program, or are “imposed in the implementation of a
land use regulation or system of land use regulations,
under which a government makes, or has in place formal or informal procedures or practices that permit
the government to make, individualized assessments
of the proposed use s for the property involved. ”  According to respondents, because the Board lacked discretion to grant the permit under state law, the
“individualized assessments” requirement is not met.
Even if valid, t hat argument would not supply an
adequate and independent state ground for the judgment.  Rather, it would be an alternative federal
ground to affirm the judgment, albeit predicated on a
state-law holding.  That poses no barrier to this
Court’s review.  The Kentucky Supreme Court did not

9


address the argument below, perhaps because respondents made the argument only cursorily in their
merits brief.  Supp. App. 13a.  Were this Court to reverse solely on the substantial-burden question, the
Kentucky Supreme Court could decide on remand
whether to reach that alternative argument.
Regardless, the argument is meritless.  The conditional-use permit scheme applied here requires individualized assessments; such an assessment was
performed when petitioner was initially awarded the
permit.  Pet. App. 9a.  Although the court of appeals
construed Section 10.4 of the ordinance to deny the
board discretion to grant a permit for religious structures next to non -arterial streets, Section
2000cc(a)(2)(C) is satisfied by the “implementation” of
either “a land use regulation or system of land use regulations” that entails individual assessments (emphasis added).  The “system of land use regulations”  at
issue here involves individualized assessments .  As
the Second Circuit has explained, “[b] ecause almost
all land use regimes implicate such individualized review, almost all ‘impos[itions]’ or ‘implementation[s]’
of land use regimes, 42 U.S.C. §  2000cc(a)(2)(C), will
satisfy this predicate. ”  Chabad Lubavitch of Litchfield Cnty., Inc. v. Litchfield Historic Dist. Comm’n ,
768 F.3d 183, 193 (2d Cir. 2014) (internal citation and
quotation marks omitted), cert. denied, 574 U.S. 963
(2015).  Moreover, Section 10.4 itself requires individualized assessments of what qualifies as “buildings for
the purpose of  religious worship ” and “arterial
streets,” the latter of which was disputed here, Pet.
App. 74a.
Independently, the building of the grotto—a significant construction project —with the assistance of an

10


Ohio designer, see App. 62a, affects interstate commerce, making the “individualized assessments” provision unnecessary.  42 U.S.C. § 2000cc(a)(2)(B).
In short, the meaning of the Substantial Burden
Provision was squarely decided below in a way that
deepens a longstanding conflict —now joined by the
Third Circuit.  The Court should grant review to resolve it.
II. THE COURT SHOULD GRANT REVIEW ON
THE EQUAL-TERMS QUESTION
A. The Equal Terms Provision states that “[n]o
government shall impose or implement a land use regulation in a manner that treats a religious assembly
or institution on less than equal terms with a nonreligious assembly or institution.”  42 U.S.C.
§ 2000cc(b)(1).  That means what it s ays.  Unlike the
Substantial Burden Provision, the Equal Terms Provision does not let the government justify differential
treatment even under strict  scrutiny.  Although respondents complain that petitioner has not articulated a standard (BIO 34), the standard is clear in the
statutory text:  Religious institutions can be subject to
neutral criteria but cannot be singled out because of
their religious character.  The ordinance here violates
that prohibition on its face.
Even under the prevailing lower-court view that
the provision is violated only if a “similarly situated”
nonreligious entity is treated more favorably, see Pet.
32, the decision below is indefensible.  The Kentucky
Supreme Court offered no explanation for  why the
many secular entities that the ordinance exempts
from the arterial -street requirement  are differently
situated from houses of worship .  Although respondents string together various snippets from the opinion

11


below to suggest that the Kentucky Supreme Court
concluded that the ordinance draws a “traffic -based
line” (BIO 34-35), the opinion says nothing of the sort.
It defies common sense to think that churches, synagogues, and shrines pose more traffic problems than
public schools, golf courses, rec centers, libraries, and
country clubs.
In reality, the Kentucky Supreme Court held that
RLUIPA permits the ordinance merely because some
nonreligious uses are also subject to the arterial -
street requirement and because some religious uses
(parochial schools) are not.  That approach has no
mooring in the statutory text and is less protective
than every other appellate court ’s approach  to the
question.
B.  Respondents assert (BIO 29) that “[n]ine of the
ten circuits” to address the Equal Terms Provision
agree on a non-religious comparator approach , but
concede (BIO 30) wide variation in what that standard
means, including on questions as fundamental as
which party bears the burden.  Although respondents
cite jurists who see these divisions as insignificant,
Judges Sykes, Jordan, and Thapar have flagged their
importance.
C.  No vehicle problem disfavors review of the second question presented.  Respondents argue (BIO 35)
that petitioner first fully raised the argument in the
Kentucky Supreme Court.  But that court resolved it
on the merits.  Pet. App. 17a-19a, 27a-29a.  There are
no facts to develop because the unequal treatment is
clear on the face of the ordinance, and the meaning of
the ordinance was addressed by three levels of Kentucky courts (as the petition correctly states, Pet. 36).
See Pet. App. 28a-29a, 45a-46a, 59a.  If the Court concludes any state-law questions are relevant under the

12


standard it adopts , it could remand on those questions.
At minimum, if the Court concludes that additional analysis from the Kentucky Supreme Court is
necessary, it should grant, vacate, and remand for further consideration.  The Court should not let stand a
decision that on its face misapplies the Equal Terms
Provision in a manner that no other court has endorsed.

13


CONCLUSION
The petition for a writ of certiorari should be
granted.
                 Respectfully submitted,

APPENDIX A
COMMONWEALTH OF KENTUCKY
SUPREME COURT
————

MISSIONARIES OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST, INC.

v.
JOEL FREDERIC AND ELIZABETH FREDERIC
Appellees

Appeal from Kenton Circuit Court
Honorable Patricia M. Summe, Chief Circuit Judge

OPENING BRIEF OF APPELLANT MISSIONARIES
OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST, INC.
*  *  *
b. The Board’s Denial of Saint John’s Permit to
Construct a Shrine Would Have Constituted a
Substantial Burden
The religious exercise in this case is constructing a
shrine (in the form of a grotto) in accordance with the
church’s namesake—Our Lady of Lourdes on church
property. Denying Saint John’s ability to construct its
shrine, as Appellees suggest, would act as a complete
prohibition of Saint John’ s religious exe rcise under

2a
RLUIPA. Because it would “effectively bar” Saint
John’s religious exercise, it  necessarily constitutes a
“substantial burden.” See Haight , 763 F.3d at 559
(“The greater restriction (barring access to the
practice) includes the le sser one (substantially
burdening the practice).”).5
It is, therefore, “strange” to think about whether the
Board’s denial would merely “burden[], substantially
or otherwise, this aspect of [Saint John’s] requests”
because it would “effectively bar” Saint John’s exercise.
Id. at 564-65. Nonetheless, the Board’s denial of Saint
John’s Permit would also satisfy the “lesser
restriction” of a substantial burden, contrary to the
findings of the Court of Appeals in this case.
Other than finding that a complete bar of a religious
exercise is sufficient (but not necessary) to constitute
a substantial burden, courts have used various tests to
determine whether state or local action constitutes a
substantial burden on religious exercise. Because
“RLUIPA does not define ‘substantial burden,’ and the
term has not been delineated by the Supreme Court of
the United States[,] . . . what constitutes a ‘substantial
burden’ on religious exercise under RLUIPA has
confounded federal courts[.]” New Life Evangelistic
Center. v. City of St. Louis, 564 S.W.3d 665, 683 (Mo. Ct.
App. 2018) (citing Roman Catholic Bishop v. City of
Springfield, 724 F.3d 78, 94-95 (1st Cir. 2013)).
Federal courts focus on th e facts of each particular
religious adherent to evaluate substantial burdens on
religious exercise. In general, courts have found a
substantial burden if state or local action either (1)

5 To clarify, a “complete bar” is sufficient but not necessary to
constitute a substantial burden, and Saint John does not contend
otherwise.

3a
directly coerces or puts substantial pressure on the
religious institution to change its behavior; or (2)
causes substantial delay, uncertainty, and expense. 6
Saint John satisfies the substantial burden standard
regardless of which test this Court applies.7
As detailed below, the Board’s denial of Saint John’s
Permit would completely bar  Saint John’s religious
exercise. In the alternative, denial of Saint John’s
Permit would (1) directly coerce or put substantial
pressure on Saint John to change its behavior; and (2)
cause substantial delay, uncertainty, and expense.

6 Courts that have mentioned the coercion or substantial
pressure tests include the Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth,
Eleventh, and D.C. Circuits. See, e.g., Westchester Day School v.
Village of Mamaroneck, 504 F.3d 338, 349 (2d Cir. 2007); Davis v.
Wigen, 82 F.4th 204, 211-12 (3d Cir. 2023); Pendleton v. Jividen,
96 F.4th 652, 656 (4th Cir. 2024); Lozano v. Collier, 98 F.4th 614,
621 (5th Cir. 2024); Mustin v. Wainwright, No. 23-3671, 2024 U.S.
App. LEXIS 21896, at *10 (6th Cir. Aug. 27, 2024); Thai
Meditation Ass’n of Ala., Inc. v. City of Mobile, 980 F.3d 821, 830-
31 (11th Cir. 2020); Priests for Life v. United States Dep’t of Health
and Hum. Servs., 808 F.3d 1, 6 (D.C. Cir. 2015). The Second and
Sixth Circuits have mentioned so me form of the “substantial
delay, uncertainty, and expense” test. See, e.g., Westchester Day
School, 504 F.3d at 349; Livingston Christian Schs. v. Genoa
Charter Twp., 858 F.3d 996, 1004 (6th Cir. 2017).
7 The Seventh Circuit also created the “effectively impracticable” test, but abandoned this test after the Supreme Court of the
United States issued its opinions in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby
Stores, Inc., 573 U.S. 682 (2014) and Holt v. Hobbs, 574 U.S. 352
(2015). See Jones v. Carter , 915 F.3d 1147, 1149 (7th Cir. 2019)
(“We recognized . . . that Holt and Hobby Lobby ‘articulate[d] a
standard much easier to satisfy’ than our former search for
something rendering the religious exercise ‘effectively impracticable.’”). Nonetheless, Saint John satisfies this test because the
Board’s Permit denial would have constituted a complete
prohibition of religious exercise as articulated below.

4a
i. Denial of Saint John’s Permit Would Have Acted as
a Complete Prohibition of its Religious Exercise,
Constituting a Substantial Burden
A complete prohibition of Saint John’s shrine would
be the ultimate substantial burden on religious exercise. RLUIPA does not define the term “substantial
burden.” See 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc-5. When a provision
lacks a definition, courts generally employ tools of
“[s]tatutory construction [which] ‘begins with the
language of the statute.’” Leming v. Secretary of Health
and Hum. Servs., 98 F.4th 1107, 1111 (Fed. Cir. 2024)
(citing Hughes Aircraft Co. v. Jacobson, 525 U.S. 432,
438 (1999)). “In matters of statutory construction[,] the
duty of [a court] is to give effect to the intent of
Congress, and in doing so [a court’s] first reference is
of course to the literal meaning of words employed.”
Flora v. United States , 357 U.S. 63, 65 (1958). “In
interpreting RLUIPA, [courts] must construe its text
‘in favor of a broad protect ion of religious exercise, to
the maximum extent permitted by the terms of this
chapter and the Constitution.’” Johnson v. Baker, 23
F.4th 1209, 1214 (9th Cir. 2022) (quoting 42 U.S.C.
§ 2000cc-3(g)).
The term “burden” is generally defined as (1) “[a]
duty or responsibility”; (2) “[s]omething that is oppressive”; or (3) “[a] restriction on the use or value of land.”
Burden, BLACK’S LAW DICTIONARY 190 (7th ed. 1999).
“‘Substantial,’ in turn, is defined as ‘considerable in
quantity’ or ‘significantly great.’” San Jose Christian
College v. City of Morgan Hill, 360 F.3d 1024, 1034 (9th
Cir. 2004) (quoting Substantial, MERRIAM-WEBSTER’S
COLLEGIATE DICTIONARY 1170 (10th ed. 2002)).
Therefore, the plain, unambiguous meaning of the text
shows that a substantial burden is a “significantly
great restriction” on an institution’s religious exercise

5a
“whether or not compelled by, or central to, a system of
religious belief.” See 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc-5(7)(A).
Here, Saint John’s religious exercise is constructing
its shrine—the “Our Lady of Lourdes” grotto—on its
property next to Our Lady of Lourdes Church. The
Board’s denial of the Permit would have resulted in
Saint John’s inability to build its shrine, as conceded
by the Frederics and as determined by the Kentucky
Court of Appeals. See Frederic v. City of Park Hills Bd.
of Adjustment , No. 2022-CA-0867, 2023 Ky. App.
LEXIS 100, at *10 (Ky. App. Dec. 1, 2023) (stating that
the church is “prohibited” under the zoning ordinance
from “[c]onstruction of a grotto — large or small — in
the rear of the church property” then (incorrectly)
determining that RLUIPA does not “prohibit[] the
Board from preventing the construction of the grotto ”
(emphasis added)). Applying the literal meaning of
RLUIPA’s plain text, a complete prohibition of
religious exercise is necessarily a “significantly great”
burden on that exercise.
Case law supports a finding that a complete
prohibition is a substantial burden. The United States
Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit recently stated
that “[t]here can hardly be a more substantial burden
on a religious practice or exercise than its outright
prohibition.” Davis v. Wigen, 82 F.4th 204, 212 (3d Cir.
2023); see also Meyer v. Teslik, 411 F. Supp. 2d 983, 989
(W.D. Wis. 2006) (“It is difficult to imagine a burden
more substantial than banning an individual from
engaging in a specifi c religious practice”). Cf.
Westchester Day School v. Village of Mamaroneck, 504
F.3d 338, 349 (2d Cir. 2007) (“When a municipality
denies a religious institution the right to expand its
facilities, it is more difficu lt to speak of substantial
pressure to change religious behavior, because in light

6a
of the denial the renovation simply cannot proceed .”
(emphasis added)).
The court in Johnson v. Baker illustrates how a neartotal ban constitutes a substantial burden on religious
exercise. 23 F.4th 1209 (9th Cir. 2022). In Johnson, the
religious person was a prisoner within the Nevada
Department of Corrections. 23 F.4th at 1212. 8 The
prisoner contended that his religious exercise was the
use of scented oil during daily prayers. Id. at 1213. The
state prevented the prisone r from using scented oil
daily because the oil was only available in the prison
chapel, and the prison did not allow scented oil in
individual cells. Id. The state insisted its regulation
was valid because the prisoner could use scented oil
once a week and use unscented baby oil during the rest
of his prayers. Id. at 1212-13. Unpersuaded, the
district court found that the state’s prohibition acted
as an “outright ban” on the prisoner’s religious
exercise. Id. at 1213. The state appealed. Id. at 1214.
The Ninth Circuit explained that “RLUIPA
guarantees an ‘expansive pr otection for religious
liberty.’” Id. at 1214 (quoting Holt, 574 U.S. at 358).
And the state “grossly missed the mark” by contending
“that the use of scented oil for [the prisoner’s] prayers
[was] not really that important to his worship
practice—[and] just a mere preference.” Id. at 1215.
The court then correctly found that “[o]f course, when
a regulation ‘outright bans’ religious exercise, it
amounts to a substantial burden.” Id. at 1215 (quoting
Greene v. Solano Cnty. Jail, 513 F.3d 982, 988 (9th Cir.
2008)).

8 RLUIPA protects against substantial burdens on religious
exercise regarding prisoner inmates as well as land-use matters.
See 42 U.S.C. §§ 2000cc to 2000cc-5.

7a
The Ninth Circuit stated that “importantly, the
‘availability of alternative means of practicing religion’
has no bearing on the ‘substantial burden’ inquiry.” Id.
at 1216 (quoting Holt, 574 U.S. at 361). It was
irrelevant that the state allowed the prisoner to use
unscented prayer oil for all of his prayers. Id. The state
“regulation constitute[d] a ‘substantial burden’ on [the
prisoner’s] particular religious exercise ,” because the
state action “limit[ed] his use of scented oil . . . to a
paltry one out of 35 prayers per week.” Id. (emphasis
added).
Similarly, in Haight v. Thompson, the United States
Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit found that
barring access to a religiou s exercise intrinsically
constituted a substantial burden under RLUIPA. 763
F.3d 554, 565 (6th Cir. 2014). In Haight, five death-row
inmates filed suit under RLUIPA for a variety of
religious-based reasons. 763 F.3d at 558. The relevant
issue on appeal was whether RLUIPA gives inmates “a
right to buffalo meat and other traditional foods for a
faith-based once-a-year powwow.” Id. at 558-59.
Importantly, the court stated that under the
circumstances of that case “it [was] strange to
think . . . in terms of the prison burdening,
substantially or otherwise, this aspect of the inmates’
ceremonial requests. For the prison barred access to
the foods altogether.” Id. at 565 (emphasis added). “The
greater restriction (barring access to the practice)
includes the lesser one (s ubstantially burdening the
practice).” Id. It was irrelevant that the state allowed
prisoners “to have some traditional foods . . . but not
others[.]” Id. “When prison officials ‘place[] substantial
pressure on an adherent to modify his behavior and to
violate his beliefs,’ or ‘effectively bar’ his sincere faithbased conduct, they necessarily place a substantial

8a
burden on it.” Id. (citations omitted). The prison’s
denial of the inmates’ specific food request effectively
barred their religious exercise and required them to
“‘modify [their] behavior’ by performing less-thancomplete powwows with less-than-complete meals.” Id.
Here, like Haight, it is “strange” to think about this
“burdening, substantially or otherwise, this aspect of
[Saint John’s] requests” because the Board’s denial of
the Permit would “effectively bar” Saint John’s
religious exercise. 763 F.3d at 565. Yet, it is undisputed
that it is Saint John’s sinc ere faith-based conduct to
construct the “Our Lady of Lourdes” shrine next to Our
Lady of Lourdes Church, and denial of the Permit
would “effectively bar” this exercise.9
Further, the proposed local action in this case is even
more onerous than Johnson v. Baker , 23 F.4th 1209
(9th Cir. 2022). Unlike the prisoner’s ability in Johnson
to use scented oil a “paltry” one time per week, the
Board’s denial of Saint John’s land use Permit in this
case would have constituted a complete prohibition. It
is the equivalent of prohibiting altogether the
prisoner’s use of scented oil in Johnson, not just
restricting the prisoner’s use to one time per week. And
“[o]f course,” state action that “‘outright bans’ religious
exercise, . . . amounts to a substantial burden.”
Johnson, 23 F.4th at 1215.

9 See also In re Young, 82 F.3d 1407 (8th Cir. 1996) (finding a
substantial burden under RFRA when a trustee of a bankrupt
church attempted to recover donations because it would
“effectively prevent the debtors from tithing” for that year even
though in that case “tithing [was a] religiously motivated, but not
religiously compelled, practice”), reinstated by 141 F.3d 854 (8th
Cir. 1998).

9a
Because denial of the Permit would constitute a
complete prohibition of Saint John’s religious exercise,
this Court should find that it necessarily constitutes a
“substantial” burden, which would have required the
Board to satisfy strict scrutiny for a denial of the
Permit. The ability or inability to engage in other
forms of religious exercise does not change this
analysis. The plain text of RLUIPA and various court
opinions support this conclusion. Alternatively, the
Board’s denial of Saint John’s Permit would also
constitute a substantial burden according to standards
employed by various federal courts. Specifically, the
Board’s denial of Saint John’s Permit would (1) coerce
and put substantial pressure on Saint John to change
its behavior; and (2) cause substantial delay,
uncertainty, and expense, as demonstrated below.
ii. Denial of Saint John’s Permit Would Have
Amounted to Coercion and Inflicted Substantial
Pressure on Saint John
The Board’s denial of Saint John’s Permit would
amount to coercion and substantial pressure on Saint
John to modify its behavior. Then-Judge Gorsuch of the
United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
illustrated something akin to coercion and substantial
pressure in Yellowbear v. Lampert, 741 F.3d 48 (10th
Cir. 2014).
*  *  *
iii. Denial of Saint John’s Permit Would Have Caused
Substantial Delay, Uncertainty, and Expense
Another test that some courts employ is the
“substantial delay, uncertainty, and expense” test.
Perhaps most relevant in this case is the United States
Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit’s variation.
Relevant factors include (1) “whether the religious

10a
institution has a feasible alternative location from
which it can carry on its mission”; (2) “whether the
religious institution will suffer ‘substantial delay,
uncertainty, and expense’ due to the imposition of the
regulation”; and (3) whether the institution “has
imposed a burden upon itself.” Livingston Christian
Schs. v. Genoa Charter Township, 858 F.3d 996, 1004
(6th Cir. 2017).
An opinion published in 2023 illustrates the Sixth
Circuit’s interpretation of its own test. In Catholic
Healthcare International, Inc. v. Genoa Charter
Township, the religious organization’s “mission [was]
to further the work of Saint Padre Pio—the patron
saint of healing.” 82 F.4th 442, 445 (6th Cir. 2023).
Catholic Healthcare International, Inc. (the “Church”)
informed the Genoa Charter Township (the “Township”)
via email that it planned to create an outdoor prayer
trail on the Church’s own property. Id. at 444-45. The
Township responded by stating that it would treat the
Church’s request as the construction of a building,
requiring a permit application and approval. Id. at
445. The Church asked the Township to allow it to
proceed without a permit, but the Township refused.
Id.
*  *  *
During the apparition, the Blessed Virgin Mary
requested Saint Bernadette “to tell the priests to build
a chapel” next to the grotto. C ATHOLIC NEWS AGENCY,
supra note 1. Likewise, the priests of Saint John
believe it is God’s will to build this shrine—a smaller
replica of the French grotto—on its property next to
Our Lady of Lourdes Church. See r. at 230.
All of the Sixth Circuit factors support a finding of a
substantial burden in this case. Saint John has no

11a
feasible alternative location from which it can carry on
this particular mission, and neither party has stated
otherwise. Cf. r. 223-26. Saint John’s property is unique
because it contains the church building next to the site
of the proposed shrine. See Times of Celebrations,
Lourdes Sanctuaire (2012), https://www.dom.edu/site
s/default/files/pdfs/RCAS_Adm-Aid/StAbroad_Sanctu
ary_LadyLourdes_depliant_saison.pdf (showing the
proximity of the grotto in Lourdes, France to the
Basilica, which is a special type of church in
Catholicism).
The Board’s denial would have also caused Saint
John to suffer substantial delay, uncertainty, and
expense. The Board knew that Saint John originally
planned to construct a larger grotto, and Saint John
voluntarily submitted approval for a smaller version.
Flash Drive, Ex. 6, at 01:32:25-01:32:45 (indicating
that the board member was “relieved that it is a
smaller version of what was first mentioned,” and that
the shrine “fits so well with the Community”); see also
id. at 00:31:50-00:33:56 (discu ssing the reduction in
size).

What evidence did Appellant adduce to meet their
burden to demonstrate a “prima facie ... violation of
section 2000cc of this title?” The answer was none –

13a
and that was despite a full and fair opportunity to
adduce such evidence, first in their application
materials, then at the Board of Adjustments Hearing,
and finally before the Circuit Court.
Instead, Appellant failed to present “prima facie
evidence” that the requirements that trigger the
substantial burden requirement was met. They
presented no proof that any zoning activities of the
City of Park Hills receives federal financial assistance.
42 U.S.C. § 2000cc(a)(2)(A) (“in a program or activity
that receives Federal financial assistance”).
They presented no evidence that zoning activities of
the City of Park Hills would affect commerce. 42 U.S.C.
§ 2000cc(a)(2)(B) (“affects, or removal of that substantial burden would affect, commerce with foreign nations,
among the several States, or with Indian tribes”).
And Appellant presented no evidence that there is
in place individual assessments of the proposed uses
for use variances for the property involved. 42 U.S.C.
§ 2000cc(a)(2)(C) (“system of land use regulations,
under which a government makes, or has in place
formal or informal procedures or practices that permit
the government to make, individualized assessments
of the proposed uses for the property involved”).
To the contrary, Kentucky law explicitly prohibits
use variances for anyone – which was the entire basis
of the Frederics’ appeal. KRS 100.247; Louisville &
Jefferson County Planning Comm'n v. Schmidt, 83 S.W.3d
449, 451 (Ky. 2001). In that se nse, then, at least as a
matter of record proof in this matter, it is clear that
RLUIPA does not apply. That, of course, is fatal, at
least as concerning this appeal.
